chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marar, Yunus, and Abu Bakr al-Hadrami narrated, saying:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The conduct of Ali (peace be upon him) among the people of Basra was better for his Shia than whatever the sun rose upon, for he knew that the people had power (dawlah), so if he had taken them as captives, his Shia would have been taken as captives.'

I said: 'Inform me about the Qa'im (the Awaited Imam), will he conduct himself with the same conduct?' He said: 'Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) conducted himself with leniency (mann) among them because he knew of their power, and indeed the Qa'im will conduct himself among them contrary to that conduct, because they have no power.'

key_terms.الْقَائِم: the Qa'im, referring to the Awaited Imam (peace be upon him)
key_terms.بِالْمَنِّ: with leniency, clemency, or gentle treatment

ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali's political strategy differ from that of the Qa'im regarding the people of Basra?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the strategic wisdom (*hikmah*) of Imam Ali in Basra, where his leniency was a calculated political move to shield his followers from the consequences of the prevailing power dynamics. It establishes a theological parallel with the Mahdi, whose conduct will be defined by absolute authority and the absence of such political constraints, reflecting the shift from a context of shared power to one of divine dominion. This contrast underscores the Shia understanding of how leadership adapts to the specific *dawlah* (power structure) of the time.
